facts.title: A miracle the size of a wall
facts.body: Veronese painted The Wedding Feast at Cana for the refectory of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice (1563). Now in the Louvre, the canvas is immense — a Venetian banquet dressed as the Gospel miracle where water becomes wine.

facts.title: Christ among the guests
facts.body: Jesus sits near the center of the long table, marked more by composure than theatrical glow. The miracle unfolds as social theater: divinity visiting a wedding at festival pitch.

facts.title: Mary prompts the miracle
facts.body: Mary, seated near Christ, is the quiet catalyst — she notices the wine has failed. Veronese keeps her dignified inside a crowd that otherwise threatens to swallow the narrative.

facts.title: The bridal pair
facts.body: Bride and groom occupy places of honor along the feast. Their celebration is the pretext for the first public sign in John’s Gospel — hospitality stretched until heaven intervenes.

facts.title: A foreground orchestra
facts.body: Musicians play at the lower center of the canvas. The banquet becomes audition and feast at once — Venice hearing itself celebrate.

facts.title: Veronese in the band
facts.body: Tradition identifies Veronese himself among the string players, with fellow Venetian painters as companions. The miracle scene doubles as a self-portrait of art’s city.

facts.title: Jars of new wine
facts.body: Large stone jars recall vessels of Jewish purification rites that Christ orders filled with water. Servants tip and pour at the lower edge — the miracle made tangible as logistics.

facts.title: Silver, glass, and appetite
facts.body: The table groans with vessels, fruit, and ruffled linen. Veronese turns Eucharistic overtones into sensory overload — tasting, seeing, and hearing all at once.

facts.title: A stage of columns
facts.body: Classical colonnades and balustrades lift the feast into fantasy antique grandeur filtered through Venetian taste. Architecture here is pageantry — depth as spectacle.

facts.title: Hands that make the miracle work
facts.body: Servants crouch and pour in the foreground, bridging sacred narrative and kitchen reality. Veronese insists wonders still need people willing to fill jars.

facts.title: The steward tastes the wine
facts.body: The steward who tastes the transformed wine stands for astonished hospitality staff — bureaucracy meeting miracle. John’s Gospel needs this witness to declare the wine better than before.

facts.title: Spectators above the feast
facts.body: Figures lean from balustrades and terraces, turning the wedding into a public Venetian event. Looking becomes part of the composition’s social physics.

facts.title: Plate that flashes wealth
facts.body: Silver and glass catch Veronese’s light like jewelry. Luxury is not background — it is the worldly stage on which a sacred surplus of wine arrives.

facts.title: Animals under the banquet
facts.body: Dogs nosing under the table keep the feast grounded in messy life. Even miracles happen in rooms that still smell like kitchens.

facts.title: Stone order behind revelry
facts.body: Paired columns and cornices impose classical order on the chaos of guests. Veronese’s architecture frames appetite without scolding it.

facts.title: Timekeeping on the table
facts.body: Still-life details — including timepieces in related banquet traditions — remind viewers that feasts end. Here abundance is urgent: drink while the miracle lasts.
